profile.name: Krishnanattam
profile.tagline: Kerala's sacred eight-night dance drama of Krishna
profile.insight: Created in 1653 by King Manaveda after a mystic vision, Krishnanattam is an eight-play temple dance drama performed exclusively by men and boys at Guruvayur, directly fathering the legendary Kathakali art form.
profile.profile: Krishnanattam is a sacred temple dance drama originating in Kerala, India, authored by King Manaveda of Kozhikode in 1653. Based on his Sanskrit text Krishnagiti, the tradition spans an eight-play cycle depicting the life of Lord Krishna from his birth to his ascension. Preserved today by the Guruvayur Devaswom, all performances are staged as ritual offerings near the sanctum sanctorum of the Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple. The performance combines four elements of classic Indian drama—Angika, Vachika, Aharya, and Satvika—featuring male performers clad in elaborate skirts, vibrant makeup, and iconic peacock-feathered headgear.
profile.profile_long:
### Origins and History
Krishnanattam was created by Manaveda (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode in northern Kerala. Completed on 16 November 1653 when Manaveda was 68 years old, the dance drama is rooted in his Sanskrit text, *Krishnagiti*. The work draws literary inspiration from the 10th and 11th skandhas of the Bhagavata Purana, Jayadeva's *Gita Govinda*, the *Sree Krishna Vilaasam Mahakavya*, and Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri's *Narayaniyam*. Legend holds that King Manaveda experienced a vision of Krishna as a child beneath an Elanji tree at Guruvayur temple. Though instructed only to view and not touch the divine child, the king embraced the vision in excitement. Krishna vanished, leaving behind a single peacock feather from his headgear, which was subsequently integrated into the crown of the character Sri Krishna. The original troupe was maintained by the Zamorin until 1958, when management transferred to the Guruvayur Devaswom. Krishnanattam is historically recognized as the direct progenitor of Kathakali.

### How It Is Danced
Performed exclusively by men and young boys as a nocturnal temple act, Krishnanattam synthesizes the four dramatic aspects defined by Bharata Muni: movement (Angika), vocal text (Vachika), costume/makeup (Aharya), and emotional state (Satvika). Performers undergo rigorous training starting around age ten for dynamic roles (vesham) and music, or age five for chutti makeup application and playing the Madhalam drum. The movement language blends physical expression with rhythmic coordination. Footwork is punctuated by ankle bells, known as chilanka, tied over leather pads below the knees for male performers and around the ankles for female characters. Dancers navigate the performance space facing the temple lamp and sanctum, embodying gods, demons, and mortals through structured choreographic patterns.

### Music and Instruments
Music in Krishnanattam relies on Sanskrit slokas and padyageethams patterned after the poetic forms of Jayadeva's *Gita Govinda*. The vocal text is supported by traditional percussion, prominently featuring the Madhalam drum. Opening with sacred slokas such as "Jagathi sukritilokai: nandithaananthidaasa", the singers provide a continuous melodic structure that drives the physical rhythm and narrative pacing of the ensemble. Musicians train for years to sync drum rhythms precisely with the expressive steps and dramatic gestures of the dancers.

### Costume and Setting
Costumes and makeup in Krishnanattam are handcrafted by the teachers and artists. Male characters wear a starched gathered petticoat beneath a white skirt featuring horizontal orange/orange-red and black stripes near the bottom. Their upper dress consists of a long-sleeved shirt open at the back, a wooden breast-plate, chest ornaments of beads and fresh flora, upper arm bands, wrist ornaments, a girdle, and shawls fitted with mirrors at each end. Female roles wear long floor-length gathered white skirts with red borders, back-tied long-sleeved blouses, wooden breast-plates covered in red cloth, and ankle bells (chilanka). Face makeup utilizes three basic colors: pazhuppu (red-dominant orange), minukku (yellow-dominant orange), and paccha (yellow-green). A chutti—two white protruding borders along the jawline—frames paccha make-up. The most sacred garment is the headgear, which comes in two primary forms: a bun (mudi) and a crown (kiriitam) topped with peacock feathers.

### Occasions and Meaning
The performance cycle consists of eight sequential plays: Avataram, Kaliyamardanam, Rasakrida, Kamsavadham, Swayamvaram, Banayuddham, Vividavadham, and Swargarohanam, remembered by the mnemonic "a-ka-ra-ka-swa-bha-vi-swa". Each play is staged as a devotional offering with specific spiritual intentions: Avataram for the birth of a child, Kaliyamardanam to remove poison, Rasakrida for the well-being of unmarried girls and marital harmony, Kamsavadham to conquer enemies, Swayamvaram for happy matrimony, Banayuddham and Vividavadham to end poverty and ensure good harvests, and Swargarohanam for the peace of a departed soul. Because concluding with Lord Krishna's demise in Swargarohanam is deemed inauspicious, Avataram is traditionally repeated on a ninth night.

### Notable Figures
The central historical figure of Krishnanattam is Samoothiri Manavedan Raja (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode. Educated by Anayath Krishna Pisharody and Desamangalath Varrier, Manaveda authored the *Poorva Bharatha Champu* in 1643 before completing *Krishnagiti* in 1653. A statue of King Manaveda stands near the 'Panjajanyam' guest house in Guruvayur to honor his creation.

### Regional Variants
Krishnanattam is intrinsically bound to the Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Thrissur district, Kerala. While the troupe has toured internationally to Europe, the United States, Singapore, and Paris, all official performances remain rooted in the lineage managed by the Guruvayur Devaswom, which employs over 70 staff members to sustain the tradition.

### Lineage
Krishnanattam directly inspired and paved the way for Kathakali, another major classical dance-drama form of Kerala. The stylistic continuity between Krishnanattam's aharya (costume and facial makeup) and angika (bodily performance) served as the structural template for Kathakali's evolution in subsequent centuries.

profile.sacred_note: Krishnanattam is a sacred ritual dance-drama performed near the sanctum sanctorum of the Guruvayur Sri Krishna temple as an offering by devotees. The headgear, especially Sri Krishna's peacock-feathered crown, is treated with extreme sacredness. Before applying make-up, actors prostrate before an oil lamp in devotion to Lord Guruvayoorappan.

teaching.rhythm: Accompanying Sanskrit slokas and padyageethams backed by Madhalam drumming
teaching.formation: Nocturnal ritual theater facing the temple lamp and sanctum sanctorum
teaching.level_notes: Requires intense early training starting as early as age 5 for percussion/chutti makeup and age 10 for performance roles.

music_profile.musical_form: Sanskrit text structured into eight dramatic plays (chapters)
music_profile.sound_description: Resonant vocal recitation of Sanskrit slokas accompanied by rhythmic Madhalam drumming, creating a solemn, sacred atmosphere suited for nocturnal temple ritual.

movement_profile.footwork: stamping feet with ankle bells (chilanka) attached to leather pads below knees for men or around ankles for women
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Proscenium-style temple court performance facing the sanctum sanctorum
movement_profile.partnering: Ensemble performance consisting entirely of men and young boys portraying both male and female roles
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not treat headgear or costume non-devotionally; sacred rituals and prayer before an oil lamp must precede performance.

episode_brief.title_hook: The King's Vision: Sacred Plays of Guruvayur
episode_brief.logline: Step inside Kerala's Guruvayur temple to explore Krishnanattam, the 17th-century sacred dance drama created by King Manaveda that gave birth to Kathakali.
beats: Night falls over the Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Kerala as oil lamps are lit.
An actor prostrates before the oil lamp, applying traditional paccha and chutti facial makeup.
The troupe adorns sacred peacock-feathered headgear, commemorating King Manaveda's 1653 vision.
Dancers execute dramatic steps punctuated by Madhalam drums and Sanskrit slokas.
The eight-play cycle unfolds as an auspicious ritual offering for temple devotees.
visual_motifs: Oil lamps burning near the sanctum sanctorum
Peacock feather adornments on high crowns (kiriitam)
Protruding white chutti jaw borders framing green paccha face paint
Layered white skirts with orange and black stripes
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An esteemed master from the Guruvayur Devaswom troupe with deep reverence for ritual performance and classical Sanskrit drama.
episode_brief.music_cue: Rhythmic Madhalam drum beats pairing with chanted Sanskrit opening slokas.

claims.text: Krishnanattam is a temple dance drama presenting the story of Krishna in eight plays created by Manaveda.
claims.quote: It is a dance drama and presents the story of Krishna in a series of eight plays and was created by Manaveda (1585–1658 AD), the then Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode

claims.text: Krishnanattam survives at the Guruvayur Sri Krishna temple and is the direct progenitor of Kathakali.
claims.quote: It survives in its glory at the Guruvayur Sri Krishna temple (Thrissur district, Kerala, India). It is a direct progenitor of the Indian classical dance drama called Kathakali.

claims.text: The eight plays follow a specific narrative order from Avataram to Swargarohanam.
claims.quote: The eight plays are: Avataram, Kaliyamardanam, Rasakrida, Kamsavadham, Swayamvaram, Banayuddham, Vividavadham and Swargarohanam.

claims.text: Peacock feathers are worn on the headgear based on King Manaveda's vision of Krishna.
claims.quote: Manaveda got one peacock feather from the headgear of Bhagavan Krishna. The peacock feather was incorporated in the headgear for the character of Sri Krishna in the dance drama Krishnanattam

claims.text: Training for performers begins at an early age.
claims.quote: Training for artists starts as early as 10 years for 'vesham' and music, 5 years for Madhalam and chutti.

claims.text: In Kerala, Krishnanattam dramas are danced exclusively by men and young boys.
claims.quote: Au Kerala, les drames sont dansés uniquement par des hommes et de jeunes garçons.

claims.text: The art form is maintained as a living tradition by the Guruvayur Devaswom.
claims.quote: The blessed art form is still maintained by Guruvayur devaswom and staged as an offering by devotees.
